name: Wendy Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the town's own electric department in Harlow, the same place my dad worked for thirty-one years. We do everything, new services for houses, pole changes, streetlights, and the Christmas lights on the square every December, which is my favourite job of the year. There's five of us on the line side. What I like is that I know half the people whose power I'm fixing, and they know my dad. What wears me out is being the only woman on the crew, you have to be twice as good to get half the credit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life at home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Luke, he's a mechanic at the tractor dealership, and we're getting married next autumn at St. Anne's, where my parents got married. We rent a little house on Orchard Lane and we've got about three months put by, plus the wedding money my parents are helping with. I don't use those AI programs, I don't trust them. My dad still calls me after every storm to ask if I wore my gloves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and good. Honest work doesn't come from a computer. I'd say that at church coffee hour and probably to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, which is what I want. I'd keep my job, get married, and maybe buy a house in a few years. That's the life I've planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just carry on. Work my shifts, save for the wedding, help with the Christmas lights. I wouldn't change a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust AI. What is it about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's made by people who've never done a day's real work, selling it to people who don't need it. And it makes things up, I've heard. I'd rather ask someone who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything change for the wedding or the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if anything we'd feel better about buying sooner. Luke's had his eye on a place near the creek.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised and I'm glad, because honest work doesn't come from a computer. I'd say that at church coffee hour and to my dad.
S0.think: It means nothing changes for me, which is what I want. I'd keep my job, get married and maybe buy a house in a few years, the life I've planned.
S0.do: Carries on working her shifts with the town electric department, saving for the wedding and putting up the Christmas lights. Changes nothing about her plans.
S0.quote: Honest work doesn't come from a computer.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's identity is rooted in her hometown, her father's trade and her church wedding plans. She distrusts AI on principle, seeing it as made by people who've never done real work. The plateau is exactly the world she wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to learn a real trade, not just screens. If AI's taking office jobs, we should be pushing young people into apprenticeships. That's what I'd say to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry the town would sell the electric department to some big company that runs everything with machines. Then it's not about doing good work anymore, it's about profit. I'd still have a job, probably, but not the same one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe put a bit more aside each month. I wouldn't go learning new programs unless they made me. I'd go to the town council meetings if there was talk of selling the department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like seeing clouds coming over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the town might hire a big company. Is that a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's come up before. Every few years somebody on the council says we could save money by letting the big utility take over. So far the town's said no. With all this new stuff, they might say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, "Keep your head down and do good work, and they'll always need you." He's said that my whole life. I hope he's right.

S1.say: I'd say people need to learn a real trade, not just screens. If AI takes office jobs, we should push young people into apprenticeships.
S1.think: Privately I'd worry the town would sell the electric department to a big company that runs everything with machines. I'd probably still have a job, but not the same one.
S1.do: Keeps working and puts a bit more aside each month. Avoids new software unless required and attends town council meetings if selling the department comes up.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like clouds coming over the hill.
S1.quote: Keep your head down and do good work, and they'll always need you.
S1.fieldNote: Her deepest worry isn't robots on poles but the town selling its electric department to a large company. True to her outlook, her answer is apprenticeships and real trades. Her father's advice frames how she thinks about security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when big companies get to do whatever they want without anyone stopping them. I'd say it in church and to anyone who'd listen. We'd have to pull together as a town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be terrified. If a robot can do my job and Luke's, what are we going to live on? Two years is nothing, I couldn't learn anything else in two years even if I wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything. No honeymoon, a small wedding at the church hall instead of the barn venue. I'd try to stretch the savings, and I'd lean on family, Luke's parents have a farm and we could move in there if we had to. Our church would help too, that's what it's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like I'd lose the life I've been building since I was a kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, that's not up to a robot. But small. Just family and the church people, a potluck in the hall. My mum would cry, but she'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't want to. I'd try family and church first. If it came to it, I'd take what I had to, but I wouldn't like it, and I'd get off it as fast as I could.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when big companies do whatever they want with no one stopping them. I'd say it in church and that we'd have to pull together as a town.
S2.think: Honestly I'd be terrified. If a robot can do my job and Luke's, I don't know what we'd live on, and two years is nothing to learn anything else.
S2.do: Cuts everything, dropping the honeymoon and holding a small church-hall wedding instead of a barn venue. Stretches savings and leans on family and church, ready to move onto Luke's parents' farm if needed.
S2.feel: Scared, like losing the life she's been building since she was a child.
S2.quote: We'd still get married, that's not up to a robot.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Wendy's fear shows; her and Luke's jobs both look exposed. The wedding survives but shrinks, and family and church come before government. She'd take public help only as a last resort and briefly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get ready, and churches and families need to look after each other. I'd also say the town should keep its own electric department and not sell out. That's what I'd push for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still the end of my job, just not straight away. I'd get married, have a few years, and then hope they still need a few people to go up when the robots break. My dad says there's always something that breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding, a bit smaller than we'd planned. We'd save hard, try to get to six months. I wouldn't do any courses yet, I'd want to see what's happening first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be on my mind a lot, but I'd have time to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years feel very different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Two years is a flood. Five years, at least you can get married and save and see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it was a proper apprenticeship, like with real people teaching. Not on a computer. But I'd wait until I knew what was actually needed.

S3.say: I'd say people need to get ready, and churches and families need to look after each other. I'd also push for the town to keep its own electric department.
S3.think: I think it's still the end of my job, just not straight away. I'd hope they still need a few people to go up when the robots break, because my dad says something always breaks.
S3.do: Goes ahead with a slightly smaller wedding and saves hard toward six months. Holds off on courses until she sees what's needed, open only to a hands-on apprenticeship taught by people.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with room to breathe.
S3.quote: Two years is a flood. Five years, at least you can get married and save and see it coming.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Wendy keep her wedding and her sense of order. She pins her hope on her father's belief that something always breaks. She'd consider retraining only through a person-led apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to be sensible about it, as long as people don't wait for the government to fix everything. Families and towns have to plan. I'd say that kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be nervous. Ten years is long, but I want to have kids in that time, and I want to know I can provide for them. I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd want to still be doing honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as they need me. We'd get married next autumn like we planned, and probably buy the place by the creek. I'd keep savings up, and if things got close, I'd look at a hands-on job nearby, maybe at Luke's dealership fixing the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away that I can mostly live my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In ten years you might have a family. Does that change how you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, very. I'd want to be home more, and know there's money coming in. That's the main thing, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your kids, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn a trade and to work with their hands. Even if robots do a lot, I want them to know how things work. My dad taught me that, and I'd teach them.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to be sensible, as long as people don't wait for the government to fix everything. Families and towns have to plan.
S4.think: Privately I'd still be nervous, because I want to have children in that time and know I can provide for them. At thirty-seven I'd want to still be doing honest work.
S4.do: Keeps working as long as she's needed, marries next autumn and probably buys the house by the creek. Keeps savings up and, if the change gets close, looks at hands-on local work such as fixing robots at Luke's dealership.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off to mostly live her life.
S4.quote: I'd want them to learn a trade and to work with their hands.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Wendy's life plan stays largely intact: wedding, house and children. Her biggest worry becomes providing for a future family. The idea of fixing robots at Luke's dealership was her own, a surprising step for someone so wary of tech.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it could take my job and Luke's before we're even married. What would help is the town keeping its electric department and keeping people on, and apprenticeships for whatever the new jobs are. Families and churches would do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People think it's old-fashioned, but if all this happened, it's the church that would be making casseroles for families who lost their jobs. The tech companies won't be.

headlineQuote: It's the church that would be making casseroles for families who lost their jobs. The tech companies won't be.
portrait: Wendy Walsh is a 27-year-old lineworker for the town electric department in Harlow, where her father worked for thirty-one years, and the only woman on her five-person crew. She's engaged to Luke, a mechanic, with a church wedding planned next autumn and about three months saved. She distrusts AI, values hard work and apprenticeships, and turns to family and church before government. She's calm in the mild picture, alarmed by AGI in two years when both their jobs look exposed, and with more time keeps her plans for marriage, a house and children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it could take her job and Luke's before they are even married.
whatWouldHelp: The town keeping its own electric department and its staff, and apprenticeships for the new jobs, with families and churches doing the rest.
